
Fujisan Sengen Faith (富士浅間信仰)

[[File:Asamano Ookami.jpg|thumb|250px|right|'''Asama Daibosatsu's resting place stone monument located on the upper part of the Hitoana, regarded as the residence of the deity (Hitoana Fuji-kō Ruins)''']]'''Fuji Faith''' (富士信仰) is a Shinto belief (Shinto Faith) in the deity of Mount Fuji. It is one of the forms of Mountain Worship.

== Overview ==
[[File:Fujinomiya Hongu Sengen Taisha Honden.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha]]Fuji Faith involves the veneration and worship of Mount Fuji in some form – for example, regarding the mountain itself as a deity. A representative form is '''Asama Faith''' (浅間信仰, also known as '''Fuji Asama Faith'''). Other notable forms include Murayama Shugendo and Fuji Sect.
{{main|Murayama Shugendō|Fujiko (religion)}}[[File:Omuro＿Sengen＿Shrine.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Fujiyama Shimomiya Komuro Asama Shrine. A form of worship of Mount Fuji is observed.]]

When broadly dividing the history of Fuji Faith, one finds: an initial era of primitive mountain worship – when shrines began to be established to enshrine the mountain deity (called "Fukujishin" in Fudoki of Hitachi Province, "Reimoya Shin-kōmon" in the Manyōshū, and "Asama Daimyō" in Tsuruga's Fujisan Chronicle); an era in which Buddhism entered Japan and developed as a form of mountain forest Buddhism integrating earlier kami-worship concepts, marked by the appearance of ascetics (called Fuji Dōsha) whose mountain training took on a sacred mountain character; an era during the late Heian period when mountain ascetics became more organized and established sacred training sites; an era from the Nanbokuchō period and the Muromachi period in which common people increasingly climbed Mount Fuji as Fuji pilgrims or as part of the Fuji Sect; and finally, the era from the Bakumatsu and Meiji periods onward, characterized by the age of Sect Shinto.<ref name="sato">『Folk Religion』 Volume 2, p.117 "Various Aspects of Mountain Worship in Local Communities" by Sato Eiichi, Tōkyōdō Publishing, 1989</ref>

== Asama Faith ==
This section details Asama Faith in particular. Early on, the idea of worshipping Mount Fuji itself emerged, and shrines dedicated to the mountain deity, Asama Daimyō, were established in various regions at the foothills of the mountain.<ref name=sato/> Asama Faith originates from this tradition.

The core of Asama Faith is the Asama Shrine, a shrine enshrining Asama Daimyō – regarded as the spirit of Mount Fuji. Approximately 1,300 such shrines (Fuji shrines) are distributed nationwide, mainly in Shizuoka Prefecture and Yamanashi Prefecture. The primary shrine is considered to be Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha (located in Fujinomiya City, Shizuoka Prefecture), which covers most of the area above the 8th station of Mount Fuji (see details at Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha).<ref>Tōguchi Honmitsu Fuji Asama Shrine in Suntō District and Oyama Town, or alternatively Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine in Fujiyoshida City, are also considered primary by some views.</ref> Note that the original shrine of Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha, Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha Yamamiya Asama Shrine, is a rare form of shrine that does not possess a main building, exemplifying the ritual style of Fuji Faith.

It is generally held that Asama Daimyō is none other than Princess Konohananosakuya. The reason why the enshrined deity of Asama Shrines came to be identified with Konohananosakuya-hime is attributed to her involvement in the myth of her birth (as recounted in the Kojiki, specifically the section Konohananosakuya-hime's Birth), which led to her association with fire – being identified as the deity of flame (Fire God) after a miraculous birth in fire. However, according to the shrine legend of Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha, she is regarded as a water deity (Water God) who calms fire. The exact time when Mount Fuji's deity came to be identified with Konohananosakuya-hime remains unclear. In many Asama Shrines, the primary deity is alternatively Ōyamatsumi (Great Mountain Deity), the father of Konohananosakuya-hime, or Iwanagahime (Rock Long Princess), her sister. Some Asama Shrines also feature a distinctive complex shrine structure known as Asama-zukuri. Through syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism, Asama Daimyō is also sometimes called Asama Daibosatsu.

Mount Fuji has frequently erupted, causing damage to the people living at its foothills. Consequently, many Asama Shrines enshrine Konohananosakuya-hime as the sacred body (Sacred Object) to appease volcanic activity, considering her as either a fire deity or a deity of water virtue.

=== Etymology of "Asama" ===
There are various theories regarding the etymology of the name of Asama Shrines.<ref>Miyaji Naoki『History of Asama Shrines』, Meicho Publishing</ref>
* One theory posits that "asama" is an archaic word referring to a volcano.
* Another theory suggests that "Asama" designates a fierce, fiery deity – and during the Edo period Mount Fuji (a volcano) and Asama-yama were regarded as the same deity.
* A third theory claims that "Asama" signifies Aso Mountain, the result of a Kyushu-origin legend fusing with primitive faith.
* Yet another theory holds that "Asama" derives from the Ainu language, meaning either "a burning rock that emits fire" or "the depths of a swamp." In Southeast Asian languages, similar words related to volcanoes or hot springs exist – for example, in Malay, "asa" means "smoke" and "ma" means "mother," and these were applied to Mount Fuji.
* Finally, one theory suggests that when Sakanoue no Tamuramaro relocated Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha to its present site, he sought a new shrine name. At that time, many cherry trees grew naturally around the Yūtama Pond of Asama Taisha, and because of the strong association with cherry blossoms at the subsidiary shrine (Sessha) of Ise Grand Shrine – namely, Asakuma Shrine (Ise) – the local people began referring to it as "Asama no Kaminoyashiro," and thus the name was adopted for Asama Shrines.

== History ==
=== Establishment of Fuji Faith ===
In the region surrounding Mount Fuji, several ritual sites from the late Jomon period – such as the Sengo ruins (in Fujinomiya City, Shizuoka Prefecture) and the Ushiishi Ruins (in Tsuru City, Yamanashi Prefecture) – have been excavated. These sites feature arrangements of stones (Stone Circles, known as "haishi") and have been argued by scholars to be related to Fuji Faith.<ref name="fujisengen">unknown, date=August 2014</ref> If correct, this suggests that the prototype of Fuji Faith existed at least prior to the Jomon period.

The popularization of mountaineering was a major factor in garnering popular devotion to Mount Fuji. One of the earliest records of climbing the mountain is attributed to Ascetic.
The Nihon Genpō Zen'aku Reii-ki states, "At night, proceeding to Suruga and ascending the peak," indicating a connection between the ascetic and Mount Fuji. Similarly, in the Fujisan Chronicle attributed to Tsuruga, it is recorded, "There once was an ascetic who managed to climb its summit," showing numerous accounts linking the ascetic to Mount Fuji.

A figure known as the "Founder of Mount Fuji's Opening" is Matsudai, the Senior Monk. In the Honchō Seiki (compiled by Shin-sei), it is stated: "There was a monk in Suruga Province called Fuji Shōnin, whose name was Matsudai; he ascended Mount Fuji several hundred times and constructed a Buddha pavilion at the summit, known as Dainichiji." His act of building a temple at the summit is seen as a manifestation of his faith—a significant turning point in Fuji Faith. Matsudai is also regarded as the organizer of Shugendō, and his influence played a major role in the evolution of Fuji Faith.

In the Jizō Bosatsu Reigenki (compiled by Jitsuei), it is written: "They call him Matsudai. He worshipped the sacred peak of Fuji in Suruga Province…" (excerpt omitted) – this passage suggests a connection between Matsudai and Murayama Shugendo, leading to the view that Matsudai established Murayama Shugendo.<ref name="fujisengen">Hirano Eiji, Fuji Asama Faith, Yūzankaku Publishing</ref> Murayama Shugendo is one of the earliest organized expressions of Fuji Faith among the people.

Furthermore, in the late Heian period, the Ryōjin Hishō (compiled by Emperor Go-Shirakawa) states, "The sacred sites in all directions include, among others, the mountain of Fuji in Suruga and its training grounds…" indicating that by the end of the Heian period, Mount Fuji was already an object of devotion.<ref name="fujisengen"/></ref>

=== Bestowal of Divine Rank to Asama Daimyō ===
In the Nihon Buntoku Tennō Jitsuroku (compiled by Fujiwara Mototsune and others), it is recorded that in the 3rd year of Jinju (853 AD), Asama Kami was elevated to the Rank of a renowned deity.

Furthermore, in the Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku (compiled by Fujiwara Tokihira and others), it states, "In Suruga Province, Asama Kami was Ranked as Shōsanmi," indicating that in the 1st year of Jōgan (859 AD), he was promoted to the Rank of Shōsanmi.

Also, the same source records, "In Fuji District, the Great Mountain of Asama Daimyō, holding the Rank of Shōsanmi…" From these records, it is inferred that the state, in order to curb volcanic activity, had Asama Kami enshrined – which eventually became the present-day Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha.<ref>{{Cite book|language=ja|author=Kubota Atsushi|title=Fuji: The Source of Faith and Art|year=2009|publisher=Shogakukan|pages=24}}</ref> Thus, it is believed that the first shrine related to Mount Fuji was established in Suruga Province.<ref name="fujisengen"/></ref>

In the report from the 6th year of Jōgan (864 AD) in August, it is recorded: "A low-Ranking official from Kai Province stated that the fire of Mount Fuji in Suruga was determined by divination using turtle shells, and that the enshrined priests and officials of Asama Myōjin were duly observing ritual purity." This shows that in Suruga Province there were already priests and officiants enshrining "Asama Myōjin."

In the report from the 7th year of Jōgan (865 AD) in December, it is recorded: "An Asama Myōjin shrine established in Yatsushiro District of Kai Province was listed as an official shrine, with appointed priests and officials, and rituals were conducted regularly." This served as a turning point for the establishment of Asama Shrines on the Kai side as well. Thus, due to concerns over eruptions, Asama Faith gradually expanded.

Note that the names "Asama Kami", "Asama Daimyō", and "Asama Myōjin" vary according to era and record.

=== Relationship with Shugendō ===
In the Yoshitsune-ki (author unknown), it is written: "When the yamabushi met and discussed the peak of enlightenment, the state of Mount Shakyamuni Tathāgata, the significance of the Eight Great Kongo Children, as well as the peak of Fuji and the prayers of the yamabushi, someone would answer with dazzling clarity…" indicating that the relationship between Mount Fuji and Shugendō was widely recognized.<ref name="fujisengen"/></ref>

== Shrines Involved in Fuji Faith ==
* Komagome Fuji Shrine (located in Tokyo Metropolis, Bunkyo Ward, Hon-Komagome) – One of the oldest Fuji Sect organizations, established by the Town Fire Brigade. The famous proverb "One Fuji, Two Hawks, Three Eggplants" is said in modern times to originate from this shrine, although no documentary evidence exists to support this theory. According to this modern theory, the origin is attributed to the presence of a Falconer's Mansion in the vicinity and the local specialty of the Komagome Eggplant.

== Others ==
Although not directly related to Fuji Faith, Nichiren Buddhism and Fuji Monryū (also known as Nikkōmonryū) are also based on Mount Fuji. Following the dying wish of the sect founder Nichiren, who stated that "the main ritual platform of the sect should be established on Mount Fuji (summary)," Daishiji Temple was built at the foot of Mount Fuji. Moreover, influential temples and sects established by Nichiren's prominent disciple Nikkō and his followers – namely, Kamijō Daishiji Temple, Kitayama Honmonji Temple, Nishiyama Honmonji Temple, Koizumi Kuonji Temple, and Shimojō Myōrenji Temple – are collectively known as the Fuji Five Mountains.

Although not directly connected with Fuji Faith, Mount Fuji is still widely regarded as a sacred site in modern times. New religious movements such as Hakkō Shinboku-kai, Aum Shinrikyo, and Hō no Hana Sanbōgyō have established bases there.
